newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Northern Afghan warlord recognises ousted government.
newsitem.headline: Northern Afghan warlord recognises ousted government.

text.p: SALANG PASS, Afghanistan, Oct 14 (REUTER) - A powerful Uzbek warlord recognised Afghanistan's ousted goverment on Monday, but held back from joining a military alliance with its forces around Kabul.

"We recognised Mr. (Burhanuddin) Rabbani's government," a spokesman for the northern leader, Abdul Rashid Dostum, told reporters after a five-hour-long meeting of the principals at the top of the Salang Pass north of Kabul.

"We (also) set up a commission today to consider the proper roles and responsibilities of the (Dostum forces) in the government as well as those of other parties," the spokesman, General Mohamed Youssef, added.

General Dostum, estranged from the Rabbani government and especially from Rabbani's Defence Minister, Ahmad Shah Masood, since 10994, has been much courted since insurgent Taleban forces drove the government out of Kabul little more than two weeks ago.

Dostum's recognition of Rabbani, an ethnic Tajik, as the legitimate head of state during his second meeting with Masood in a week suggests a ring of hostile forces are being set in place around the mainly Pushtun Taleban, who now occupy about two-thirds of Afghanistan.

Dostum, who speaks for the country's northern Uzbeks and Masood who is a hero to its Tajiks, was joined at the meeting by Karim Khallili who represents the Shi'ite Hazara, a people from central Afghanistan.
Also in attendance was the son of Pir Ghailani, a moderate Pushtun from the southwest who favours re-instituting the country's monarchy.

Given the broad ethnic representation at the meeting and the military strength of Dostum and Masood combined, Taleban radicals' dreams of establishing an ultra-conservative Islamic hegemony over all of Afghanistan, including non-Pushtun areas, would seem to be over.
With Masood's forces pressing the Taleban around Kabul, especially from the north, the immediate question is whether Taleban can hold on to the capital.

A Masood field commander, Abdul Bashir Salanghi, came to the meeting in the late afternoon directly from the front outside the capital and told reporters his forces had made significant progress in their attempt to recapture Kabul.
He said his forces had taken the military airfield at Bagram although Taleban still occupied a position at the end of the runway.

"We are in Parwan (a Kabul district) and along the edge of the city," Salanghi said. "We are not moving forward at the moment. Right now we are not attacking. There is an uprising of the people who are unhappy with the Taleban."

General Youssef said that there had been no decision made about joint military operations by Dostum and Masood forces but did not rule out the possibility. He said Masood had not been asked or given any commitment about his plans around Kabul.
Monday's meeting also appointed an executive committee for the defence of Afghanistan, which included Dostum, Masood, Pir Gailani and Karim Khallili.
General Youssef said that more members of the council would be appointed in the near future to represent outlying provinces in Afghanistan.

The meeting broke up at about 5.30 p.m. as the leaders emerged from a battered green metal trailer perched alongside the edge of the road below snow-capped peaks and hopped into their limousines and four-wheel drive vehicles.
The 3,300 metre pass, which links Kabul to northern Afghanistan, had been closed to regular traffic througout the day.
Once the meeting broke up, the Salang highway was filled with taxis, trucks and buses climbing laboriously north to the pass filled with refugees fleeing the fighting in the south.

Billowing black exhaust up the steep grades, sounding horns and flashing lights as they attempted to overtake one another on sharp switchbacks, the vehicles seemed to symbolise the panic in which Afghan civilians find themselves once again.
In the valleys to the south bullet-riddled pick-up trucks and abandoned tanks showed the price Taleban paid for its attempt to advance towards the Salang before being driven back.

In Jabal os Saraj, where Masood forces have a major command post, Masood soldiers strolled the streets with Kalashnikovs slung over their shoulders and tanks clanked down the main street, presumably on their way to the southern front.
